national.title: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
national.summary: The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement.
national.body:
Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press

Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press

Victoria Milko, Associated Press Victoria Milko, Associated Press

ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Work crews boxed up the venue for this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use.

The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.

In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs" the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left "to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations."

national.title: Families frustrated with Pentagon probe of deadly drone strike
national.summary: The Pentagon is preparing to release findings of its investigation into the attack that killed six U.S. soldiers in Kuwait early in the Iran war.
national.body: Gold Star families have told CBS News that briefings about a forthcoming U.S. military report on the deadliest strike on U.S. soldiers in the Iran conflict did not, to their satisfaction, address their concerns about the military preparations and response to the attack.Several of the families said they have been briefed about the unclassified results from the long-awaited internal probe into one of the first attacks on U.S. troops during Operation Epic Fury. Six U.S. Army Reserve soldiers were killed by a drone strike on their command post in Kuwait, known as Port Shuaiba, on March 1.The official report has not yet been released to the public. The Pentagon has indicated it could be made public in a matter of days. Over the past week, the Army briefed at least three Gold Star families on the investigation, and several family members told CBS News they were frustrated by what they heard. Some of those briefed told CBS News the report does little to address the findings of an eight-month CBS News investigation, in which multiple sources said Army commanders ignored repeated warnings about the drone threat in the weeks before the attack.Witnesses told CBS News that the facilities were not fortified to protect service members from a strike by one-way attack drones, which are a staple of the Iranian arsenal. Soldiers on the site said they had seen U.S. intelligence prior to the war showing the location was on an Iranian target list. And they argued the facilities lacked sufficient medical supplies and a plan for a mass casualty incident.The briefings were led by Brig. Gen. Peter Glass, the deputy commander of U.S. Army Central, according to those who attended. They were individually held at either military or National Guard posts in locations close to the respective families. "I wish I felt better," a Gold Star family member told CBS News after her briefing, which she said lasted roughly three hours. "I wish this gave me more than what I had yesterday or what I had the day before."The briefings come just days after a U.S. Army soldier who survived the deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran.The whistleblower, Army Maj. national.title: Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress'
national.summary: Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn't enter her bloodstream correctly.
national.body:
Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press

A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, "Don't let me suffer like this," during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein.

Yet Reinaldo Dennes' spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes' shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday.

"Twice he said, 'It's not working. It's not working. It's not going how it's supposed to go. This isn't right.' Those types of words kept coming," said the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent.

Dennes was "clearly in tremendous distress," said Hood, who called it torture.

It was the ninth execution this year in Texas, which has a long history of using the death penalty as punishment for murder. Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn't enter her bloodstream correctly.

Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said initial attempts to place two IV lines into Dennes' hands and arms were unsuccessful.

Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. Hernandez said an IV was successfully placed in the left side of his neck 16 minutes later at 6:20 p.m., followed by another line in his left foot at 6:38 p.m.

national.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
national.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
national.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

national.title: Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
national.summary: "The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed."
national.body:
Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.

The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia's technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.

"The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed."

WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips

Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.

The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.

national.title: Second opinion saves career of pro athlete told to amputate leg
national.summary: Doctors said his leg would need to be amputated. Here's how this athlete got back on the field after a rare diagnosis.
national.body: Henry Nell's career pushed his body to the limit. He played rugby professionally in his home country of South Africa. Then he moved to the United States and began playing arena football, an indoor version of American football played on a slightly smaller field. He played for multiple teams across two leagues, always serving as the kicker. In 2021, he began to feel some stiffness in his knee. Nell brushed it off as a strained muscle. When it didn't go away, he assumed it was a sign of aging. But in 2025, when he was playing for the Albany Firebirds, the team trainer recommended an X-ray. The scan showed a mass behind his knee. Nell tried to convince himself that it was just a cyst or a pocket of fluid. But it was diagnosed as parosteal osteosarcoma — a rare, slow-growing type of bone cancer. The tumor had been growing for years, doctors said. Hearing the word "cancer" wasn't the scariest part, Nell said. The terror came when he met with a local oncologist, who recommended amputation. "I felt like, nothing could get better, like everything's caving in. My sports career is in jeopardy. My whole rest of my life is in jeopardy," Nell recalled. "If we have to amputate the leg, what's the next 60, 70 years of my life going to be? What effect does that have on my family? Is my wife going to push me in a wheelchair? All these thoughts ran through my head. It was one of the most frightening times I've ever experienced." A second opinion and a complex plan Nell and his wife, a physical therapist, wanted a second opinion. They traveled to New York City to meet with Dr. Nicola Fabbri, a surgical oncologist and chief of the Division of Musculoskeletal Oncology Surgery at NYU Langone Health who specializes in complex limb-preserving surgeries. Fabbri proposed a plan that could let Nell treat the cancer and keep his leg. Parosteal osteosarcoma occurs at the surface of the bone. Fabbri would remove just enough bone to ensure the tumor was gone and couldn't grow back, then support Nell's knee with cadaver bone and metal plates. "We sat down for almost an hour, and the last 10 minutes of us being there, I was just in tears," Nell recalled. "I couldn't even talk to the man. I felt so bad, but I was just crying because there was hope."Fabbri felt sure he could help Nell keep his leg, but wasn't sure about his athletic career. She did not reveal what type of cancer she was treated for.Catherine disclosed in January 2025 that she was in remission about 10 months after announcing her diagnosis. At the time, she said in her post on Instagram that she remains focused on recovery: "As anyone who has experienced a cancer diagnosis will know, it takes time to adjust to a new normal."She has gradually resumed her public duties, visiting India with William earlier this month.In the trailer, Catherine says cancer changes people profoundly, and "healing is a journey. How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty."She adds that "it's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone" and "often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that."

national.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
national.summary: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
national.body:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run more than 24 hours into overtime as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

This still remains the main sticking point, along with a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not in sight.

Not all countries have the funding or capacity to do this, and at some point the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.

This means the summit would end with no deal and have to be suspended. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

Published 1 day ago Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

national.body: Mexico's military announced Saturday that it had captured a drug kingpin on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Top 10 Most Wanted List. Violence broke out in the state of Sinaloa afterwards, rattling civilians. Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, also known as "El Chapo Isidro," is allegedly the leader of the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization, which the FBI described as a "heavily armed, major drug-trafficking organization" based in Sinaloa. The cartel is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the U.S., according to the FBI, and has controlled drug production, transportation and distribution throughout Mexico. Meza-Flores and two other leaders of the organization were captured by special forces during a raid in Sinaloa on Friday night, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat announced on X. Elite military agents were able to find the targets, then arrive surreptitiously in the area, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. The agents set perimeters around a residence to prevent Meza-Flores from escaping, while also defending the area from reinforcements who could have interrupted the operation. The arresting agents were attacked with gunfire and explosives, the Mexican National Defense Secretariat said. The agents entered the house and captured Meza-Flores and the two others. The three were then evacuated to Mexico City and placed in custody. national.title: Killer robots: U.N. talks fall short of hopes for legally binding rules
national.summary: U.N. talks in Geneva have failed to deliver binding rules on autonomous weapons, as humanitarian groups warn that military AI is advancing far faster than diplomacy.
national.body:
A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption

GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."

After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.

Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.

Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .

Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.

Africa Besieged Sudanese city faces relentless drone strikes and risk of mass atrocities, U.N. warns Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.

"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."

national.title: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
national.summary: The settlement will be paid by Bayer to users who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
national.body:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits ⁠alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".

Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.

The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.

The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.

The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.

"[Friday's] final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," said Christopher Seeger, a court-appointed counsel for cancer patients in the case.

Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.

LOS ANGELES — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.

Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.

With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a "testament of the hard work" his team put into the case. He said he was "intimately familiar" with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.

Rinderknecht's attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.

"After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration," Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.

national.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
national.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
national.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

national.title: Mexican drug lord on FBI's 10 most wanted list arrested in shoot-out
national.summary: Fausto Isidro "Chapo Idisro" Meza Flores, who is accused of drug trafficking and torture, is detained after gun fight with authorities.
national.body:
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.

Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.

Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.

Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.

Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.

A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.

It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.

Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.

Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.

A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.

Frequently Asked QuestionsWhy put lemon, orange, and grapefruit in the turkey cavity? Putting citrus inside the cavity — as well as using it to flavor the butter that's spread under the skin — will impart fragrant flavor into the entire bird. The pan juices will be infused with citrus, too; pour some onto your plate for an extra source of tart, aromatic goodness.What does putting butter under the skin do? Rubbing butter directly onto the meat of the bird — rather than over the skin — is a classic way to impart as much moist juiciness as possible into every part of turkey. Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

national.summary: Don't let your work troubles follow you home. Psychologist Guy Winch shares techniques to help you stop ruminating about your nine-to-five, so you can focus on what really matters.
national.body:
Psychologist Guy Winch, author of Mind Over Grind , shares techniques to help you stop thinking about work when the day is over. Beck Harlan for NPR hide caption

If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch .

" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.

Life Kit Listen to the podcast version of this story here Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life , says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.

"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."

That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health . Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.

Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists , shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.

Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.

national.title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
national.summary: Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
national.body:
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.

Technology Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO "There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.

The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.

But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.

The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.

Understanding AI California sues OpenAI over hacking risks Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."

Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.

national.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
national.summary: A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
national.body:
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.

It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

Voting Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College . So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

national.title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
national.summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
national.body:
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."

Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."

Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

national.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
national.summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship".
national.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

local.title: NIAGARA DISCOVERIES: Benjamin Carpenter, Lockport's first mayor
local.summary: Much has been written about Benjamin Carpenter, the first mayor of the city of Lockport, but every once in awhile we should be reminded of the contributions that were made by many of our forebears who are largely forgotten. Benjamin…
local.body:
A map of Benjamin Carpenter’s quarry property at South Transit Street and State Road in 1851

Much has been written about Benjamin Carpenter, the first mayor of the city of Lockport, but every once in awhile we should be reminded of the contributions that were made by many of our forebears who are largely forgotten. Benjamin Carpenter was born on December 26, 1805 in Orange County, N.Y. His father James died sometime after 1817 and his mother Julia took Benjamin and his three brothers to New Jersey. After four years in that state, they came to Lockport in 1829.

It is not clear what the Carpenter brothers did for a living in Lockport in the 1830s, but Benjamin must have been respected enough to win a seat on the village board in 1834 as a Whig candidate. Six years later, Benjamin and his brother James opened a limestone quarry on the south bank of the Erie Canal just west of Transit Street. Although there were other quarries already in business at the time, the Carpenters’ stone was much sought after for building purposes. Over the next 50 years, the brothers furnished stone for churches, homes, public and commercial buildings, as well as for monuments. It was not only in demand in Lockport and Western New York but across the state and throughout the country.

Ann Marie Linnabery is the assistant director of the History Center of Niagara.

Ann Clutter, a lifelong resident of the Brocton, New York area, passed away on November 19, 2026, in Greenville, South Carolina, at the age of 98.

She was born on December 23, 1927, in Clymer, New York, the daughter of the late Ernest and Roberta (Fleichmann) Seavy. Ann grew up with strong family values that remained with her throughout her life, and she carried those values into every role she held as a daughter, wife, mother, grandmother, and friend. She was a graduate of Brocton High School and remained deeply connected to the community she called home for her entire life.

Ann was married to the late William Clutter, and together they built a life centered on family, hard work, and faith. She was a devoted mother to George Clutter, Larry Clutter, Douglas Clutter, Peggy Weary, Patty Delcamp, Paul Clutter, Bernadette Auffhammer, Joseph Clutter, Thomas Clutter, Cathy Deering, and Charles "Chip" Clutter. She was also blessed with many, many grandchildren, great-grandchildren, and great-great-grandchildren, each of whom brought her great joy and pride. She is also survived by her sister, Mary Murphy.

local.summary: Little did Brian Barmore know in 2018 — when he and a friend dropped by 21 Brix Winery, Portland, on little more than a whim —- that he would one day be working there, learning all about wines, and ultimately earn one of the wine industry’s highest educational honors. So impressed with that winery v
local.body:
Little did Brian Barmore know in 2018 -- when he and a friend dropped by 21 Brix Winery, Portland, on little more than a whim --- that he would one day be working there, learning all about wines, and ultimately earn one of the wine industry's highest educational honors.

So impressed with that winery visit, and with the tasting bar specialist, Chelsea, that he met, Barmore applied for a job on the winery's production team. And soon enough, he became head winemaker and ultimately enrolled in the rigorous educational program conducted by the Wine & Spirits Educational Trust (WSET). The program is considered to be the gold standard of education within the industry.

Barmore earned such a very high score in the final unit of the program's Level Four curriculum to qualify for WSET's acclaimed Certification of Merit. Fewer than 10 percent of enrollees reach this plateau. Only 15,000 people worldwide have reached that level since the WSET was founded in 1969.

WSET's Level 4 Diploma in Wines consists of six units. The five units assessed by examination are followed by a dissertation, or a 3,000-word research assignment. Instruction is online through live sessions, each of which is followed by an on-site examination. Barmore easily passed each exam in the three levels on the first try. His dissertation was on orange wines, a white grape fermented on its skin to extract some color and flavor.

Barmore was introduced to the WSET curriculum in 2023 by a friend, Jaret Kelly, a co-worker at the winery who had completed the program's Level 2 (Wine, Spirits, Beer and Sake). Completing that phase fueled Barmore's burgeoning desire to pursue Level 3, which he passed in May 2024, and to ultimately to advance to Level 4 to earn the WSET Diploma.

"As soon as I got out of the classroom, I started looking up the diploma. I knew that was very hard to accomplish (but) that really sparked my interest because I like to do challenging things," Barmore said.

"I fell in love with learning about winemaking, really enjoyed learning about new varieties, new regions and about how winetasters know the differences in wines based on where they're grown," he explained.

Even so, his Level 3 teacher cautioned him, revealing that none of her students have passed the Diploma standard. "Hearing that made me want to do that," he said.

local.title: Quattrone joins lawsuit challenging ICE agreements
local.summary: Chautauqua County is now represented in a lawsuit challenging the state’s “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.” The law bans state law enforcement agencies from entering or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE, which can deputize local law enforcement to make immigration-related arrests. Initially, 15 N
local.body:
Chautauqua County is now represented in a lawsuit challenging the state’s “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act.”

The law bans state law enforcement agencies from entering or maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE, which can deputize local law enforcement to make immigration-related arrests. Initially, 15 New York sheriffs signed onto the suit. On Thursday, Chautauqua County Sheriff Jim Quattrone was added to the list along with Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, who recently lost in his attempt to unseat Gov. Kathy Hochul, and the Nassau County sheriff and police commissioner.

"The proposed amendments could not have been made earlier," attorney Mateo Forero-Norena of the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) in his memorandum of law supporting adding the new plaintiffs, including Quattrone. "The capacity allegations are being added in light of the concerns articulated in the court's Nov. 4 order. Meanwhile, adding Sheriff Quattrone and the Nassau County parties required completing the necessary arrangements with undersigned counsel and assembling supporting materials after the original complaint was filed. Plaintiffs elected not to seek to add them while the preliminary injunction briefing was underway so as not to complicate that emergency proceeding. This motion is being filed promptly after the Nov. 4 order and before defendants' response to the complaint is due. No discovery has occurred, and the case remains at the pleading stage. Defendants do not contend that the timing of this motion constitutes undue delay. They have taken no position on the proposed amendments."

Under the 287(g) program led by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, police officers can interrogate immigrants in their custody and detain them for potential deportation.Since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, ICE had expanded the number of signed agreements it has with law enforcement agencies across the country. That prompted Democrats in the state Legislature, with support from Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James, to enact the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act. Hochul and James have defended the law as a way to protect public safety. The state has since taken legal action against Rensselaer County, the lead plaintiff in the suit, to force compliance with the new law.

Prior to 2025, only one of New York’s 62 counties had a 287(g) agreement with ICE. As of July, there were 12 local law enforcement agencies with 287(g) contracts with ICE. In July James sent letters to the 12 local law enforcement agencies in New York that had 287(g) agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), informing them that state law requires they unwind the agreements by August 25, 2026.

local.body:
Chautauqua County government is once again rallying its employees in support of United Way of Chautauqua County, continuing its workplace giving tradition which helps fund local programs and strengthen local communities.

Through their annual payroll pledges, county employees make a gift which goes to support the work of United Way -- connecting their generosity as individuals to the programs and services helping their family, friends and neighbors.

Last year, county employees collectively gave more than $17,000 - a 21% increase over the previous year.

County Executive PJ Wendel has continued to champion the partnership, recognizing the important role county employees play not only as public servants, but as members of the communities United Way serves.

"County employees see the needs of our community firsthand," Wendel said. "Their support of United Way is another way to help make sure local programs have the resources they need to serve our residents. When our employees come together to give, they are making an investment in the people and communities we serve every day."

Last year alone, United Way programs impacted the lives of local individuals 63,249 times -- an impact only possible because of the collective giving of so many workplaces and individuals.

As part of this year's campaign, United Way of Chautauqua County 2026 Campaign Co-Chair Danielle Patti joined the county-level presentation to share more about the impact of local giving -- including a personal connection which shaped her own commitment to United Way.

As a student, Patti received tutoring through a program supported by United Way donations. Years later, she returned to that organization as an employee -- which put her on a path in the education sector, working with children and families in the same types of programs she had once benefited from.

local.body:
ORCHARD PARK -- Ed Oliver bristled at the notion of the Bills’ defensive turnaround being the result of Buffalo spending the past three weeks feasting on backup quarterbacks -- and another on deck with Miami hitting town on Sunday.

“Who cares. I mean, if I got to choose who I could play I guess it would be a starter. But you don’t get to choose,” the defensive tackle said. “All we get to choose is to take advantage of our opportunities.”

The AFC-leading Bills (8-1) have certainly done that over a three-game stretch in which they’ve allowed one touchdown and a combined 28 points. That’s a marked improvement for a defense that allowed 28.5 points per outing through its first six games.

A contributing factor could well be the level of competition, with Buffalo having faced the likes of Baltimore’s Tyler Huntley and Joe Fagnano, Minnesota’s Carson Wentz and Max Brosmer, and New York Jets rookie Cade Klubnik, who took over after Geno Smith was sidelined in Buffalo’s 31-12 win last weekend.

And now come the Dolphins (1-8), with Kyle McCord set to make his second career start in place of Malik Willis.

Bills coach Joe Brady declined to speculate on the injury-filled state of the AFC East’s quarterbacks that also includes New England’s Drake Maye -- so long as Josh Allen is not among them.

A healthy Allen, the NFL’s active leader among QBs with 131 consecutive starts, is why the Bills are once again Super Bowl contenders. And Allen isn’t looking any further beyond Sunday, even with a Thanksgiving night showdown looming against Kansas City.

“This isn’t just a cakewalk. It’s a team that’s hungry. They’re looking to upset,” he said. “And the way their defense is playing gives them a shot every game they’re in.”

The Cattaraugus County Memorial and Historical Building, located

LITTLE VALLEY -- A historic building honoring Cattaraugus County’s Civil War veterans is moving closer to rehabilitation and reopening, thanks to $300,000 in grant funding secured by Citizens Advocating Memorial Preservation (C.A.M.P.).

The Cattaraugus County Memorial and Historical Building, located at 302 Court St. in Little Valley, has been the focus of preservation efforts since C.A.M.P. took ownership of the property in 2017. Through the dedication of volunteers led by President Thomas W. Stetz, the nonprofit organization has protected the building from further deterioration, secured historic designations at the state and national levels, and obtained funding to help pay for asbestos abatement and rehabilitation.

The building was listed on the New York State Register of Historic Places in 2025 and added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 12 of that year. The National Register is the nation’s official list of properties considered worthy of preservation.

The organization’s preservation efforts received an early boost in 2023 when the Cattaraugus County Legislature donated $10,000 to help secure the building’s national historic designation.

Additional funding has come from several organizations and agencies. The largest award, $246,750, was received through the New York State Environmental Protection Fund Grant Program for Parks, Preservation and Heritage. C.A.M.P. was notified of the award in December 2025.

In February 2026, the Preservation League of New York State awarded C.A.M.P. a $40,000 Preservation Opportunity Fund grant. The organization was one of only two recipients selected for funding during the 2026 grant cycle.

Caitlin Meives, director of preservation for the Preservation League, praised the group’s efforts to save the building from demolition.

local.title: THE GREAT OUTDOORS: Two great adventures in the swamp
local.summary: With the health issues I have had to deal with over the last three weeks, there have only been a couple of quick photo adventures, but they were great ones.
local.body:
With the health issues I have had to deal with over the last three weeks, there have only been a couple of quick photo adventures, but they were great ones.

I love photographing swans in flight and there is one marsh accessible by vehicle that several trumpeter swan families frequent. Not being able to walk around easily, my photography is done mostly from my vehicle so this spot is ideal. I had been working with the swans in this marsh before I ended up in the hospital but had not gotten exactly the shots I was looking for or messed up on the ones I could have gotten. So, about a week and a half into my recovery, I decided to run over and see if the swans were still using that marsh. Just as I neared the marsh a pair of sandhill cranes were leaving. Darn, just a few seconds late! There was one family of swans on the marsh and I knew there was one other family of six plus another pair of adults that were using that spot so the decision to park and wait for the possible arrival of the others was made. This would offer me some good flight shots as they came in if I did my part. Sitting was still a little painful for me at the time, but what the heck, “No pain no gain.” Maybe the others would show up soon. Well, about an hour into my wait, it happened and a group of six could be heard with their trumpeter calling, heading my way. They didn’t land on their first pass, which was great as it gave me more opportunities to “get it right” on the second circle. Things went well and I was sure good shots were gotten. Of course, the original family got all worked up when the others came in and there was a fight between the two families, which also offered some more unique shots. A short time later, the other pair of adult swans showed up and a few more flight shots were available. My stomach pain was pretty bad by then from twisting around in the seat and sitting that long, so I headed home. Later, the photos were put on the computer and reviewed. I was happy to see what was gotten.

Doug Domedion, outdoorsman and nature photographer, resides in Medina. Contact him at 585-798-4022 or woodduck2020@yahoo.com .

local.summary: The ECWA Board of Commissioners approved its 2027 budget, which includes a 5% rate increase and $78.6 million in infrastructure investments.
local.body: Erie County residents can expect to pay more for water in the new year as the Erie County Water Authority moves forward with a major investment in its water system.The ECWA Board of Commissioners approved its 2027 budget, which includes a 5% rate increase and $78.6 million in infrastructure investments.For median residential customers, the increase in water rates means just over $21 more per year, or about $1.77 a month.The quarterly Infrastructure Investment Charge for small-meter residential customers will also increase by $1.68, from $33.33 to $35.01.WATCH: Erie County water bills going up in 2027 - here's whyThe authority said the revenue will help fund system-wide improvements, including the removal of all remaining lead service lines in its service territory by the end of 2027."We're allocating $10 million to the Lead and Copper project because we're going to complete that initiative to get all the lead out of the pipes by the end of 2027," said Joyce Tomaka, chief financial officer for the Erie County Water Authority.Tomaka said the largest portion of the authority's anticipated infrastructure spending will go toward water main projects."We serve a large portion of Erie County, and so our aging infrastructure is something that we've always had to focus on," Tomaka said. "Next year we're ramping back up and getting going on a lot more main projects."Among the major investments included in the 2027 budget:$36.8 million for new water transmission and distribution mains throughout the ECWA system.$12.8 million for upgrades at the Sturgeon Point and Van De Water treatment plants.$10 million to replace remaining lead service lines.$9.8 million for technology upgrades, including cybersecurity improvements.$6.2 million for upgrades to major pump stations.$3 million for new remote radio-read residential water meters.The residential water rates will take effect January 1, 2027. The authority said the investments are part of a broader, nearly $1 billion infrastructure improvement plan extending through 2041.

entertainment.title: '70s TV Shows That Redefined What Sitcoms Could Be
entertainment.summary: Sitcoms changed forever during the 1970s, growing bolder, edgier, and more political - and these shows led the charge into that brave new world.
entertainment.body:
CBS Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover The 1970s was a tumultuous decade, with societal discourse dominated by topics like the Vietnam War, oil inflation, and civil rights. It makes sense, then, that audiences would turn to the witty, humorous worlds of sitcoms. But not every sitcom was pure escapism — some of them used comedy to explore the turbulent and controversial topics of the era, rather than shy away from them.

Despite sitcoms accounting for some of the best TV shows of the 1970s , they'd existed for a long time before then. Yet the decade saw a shift from the 1960s' wholesome, escapist portrayals of domestic life to something much bolder and edgier. For both television and the world at large, this was a transformative time.

From showcasing strong, independent women to examining the brutal realities of war, these sitcoms delivered poignant and powerful — but still funny — views on the issues of the day. Here are five shows from the 1970s that redefined what a sitcom could be.

CBS At a time when a flushing toilet could make television history , "All in the Family" stood out for changing the landscape of sitcoms. The series centered on the Bunker family, headed by crass patriarch Archie Bunker (Carroll O'Connor). His wife, Edith (Jean Stapleton), is an eternal, and somewhat naive, optimist, and their left-leaning daughter Gloria (Sally Struthers) is married to bearded liberal Michael Stivic (Rob Reiner).

This sitcom was one of the first to take an unapologetic look at serious, real-life events of the era, and it did so via the jokes themselves. Many of the running gags involve Archie's frequent political clashes with Michael, whom he often calls "meathead." He also constantly bickers with his Black neighbor George Jefferson (Sherman Hemsley). Archie's perpetual bigotry was used to lampoon some of the common prejudices of the time.

In one episode, Michael invites his friend, David (Renny Temple), a Vietnam draft dodger, to the Bunkers' for Christmas dinner. Archie, a conservative WWII veteran, is outraged by David. In a surprising turn of events, though, Archie's visiting friend, Pinky (Eugene Roche), whose son died in Vietnam, sympathizes with him, providing a surprisingly nuanced angle on one of the most contentious topics of the day.

CBS The 1970s saw the high point of second-wave feminism, while female independence in general was beginning to become part of the status quo. And one of the most prominent television shows to portray this shift in the gender imbalance was "The Mary Tyler Moore Show."

entertainment.title: This Netflix Dark Fantasy Show Boasted One Of The Most Impressive All-Star Casts Ever
entertainment.summary: Back in 2019, Netflix released a dark fantasy series filled to the brim with A-list stars - although, at first glance, you probably wouldn't know it.
entertainment.body:
Kevin Baker/Netflix Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Brought to life through the puppetry of the Jim Henson Company, "The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance" is a prequel to the 1982 movie "The Dark Crystal." While the quality of the puppetry on display deserves plenty of praise, the 10-episode Netflix series also boasts an all-star cast of actors.

The voice cast is led by Taron Egerton, Nathalie Emmanuel, and Anya Taylor-Joy. Egerton is best known for his work as the star of the Elton John musical biopic "Rocketman" and the protagonist in the "Kingsman" film franchise. Emmanuel made a name for herself on "Game of Thrones" as Missandei . Meanwhile, Taylor-Joy's work in "The Queen's Gambit" helped launch her career as a movie star. And that's just the beginning of the show's impressive ensemble.

Mark Hamill, famous for portraying Luke Skywalker in the "Star Wars" universe , is one of the most well-known names in the "Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance" cast. The dark fantasy series also stars Helena Bonham Carter and Jason Isaacs, both of whom were mainstays in the "Harry Potter" movie franchise as Bellatrix Lestrange and Lucius Malfoy, respectively. The ensemble even features actors from some of the best sketch comedy shows , including Bill Hader, Keegan-Michael Key, and Andy Samberg. Fans of the Marvel Cinematic Universe will also recognize various names in the voice cast for "The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance," such as Benedict Wong, Hannah John-Kamen, Gugu Mbatha-Raw, and Ralph Ineson, among others.

"The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance" featured two other actors from the "Kingsman" series: Mark Hamill and Mark Strong. Strong played Merlin and shared several scenes with Egerton in the first two "Kingsman" films, as their characters work together in the story. Hamill appeared in the franchise's first installment, "Kingsman: The Secret Service," as Professor Arnold, but he and Egerton didn't meet during that film. As reported by Entertainment Weekly , at San Diego Comic-Con 2019, Egerton said he was "heartbroken" about not having met Hamill during production on "Kingsman." The two, however, participated in the Comic-Con panel for "The Dark Crystal: Age of Resistance" that year, finally uniting to share their love for their new movie.

entertainment.title: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Feasting With $120M+ in Franchise’s Box Office Comeback
entertainment.summary: Lionsgate's latest title notched the fourth-best opening Friday in the six-movie dystopian series, representing a major revival after 2023's 'The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.'
entertainment.body:
Logo text The Hunger Games : Sunrise on the Reaping has begun to ignite the box office .

Lionsgate released the sixth film in the dystopian franchise in 4,018 North American theaters, and it grossed $56 million on Friday, including Thursday previews , as it heads for more than $120 million for the weekend. This would give it the fourth-best opening Friday in franchise history, besting 2015’s Mockingjay — Part 2 ($45.6 million) and 2023’s The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes ($19 million) but behind 2013’s Catching Fire ($70.9 million), 2012’s The Hunger Games ($67.2 million) and 2014’s Mockingjay — Part 1 ($55.1 million). Sunrise earned an A- CinemaScore from audiences, putting it below the A grades of the Jennifer Lawrence -led initial 2012 movie that kicked off the series and 2013’s Catching Fire but matching the A- grades of the two Mockingjay films. Related Stories Movies How 'I Play Rocky' Star P.J. Byrne Became One of Hollywood's Go-To Character Actors Beyond the Book "The Secrecy Was Insane:" The Making of 'The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping,' From Locked Safes to Original Cast's Return

The studio had projected The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping to gross north of $80 million , but other sources expected that it would collect between $100 million and $130 million, which now looks to be the case. Adapting author Suzanne Collins’ prequel novel that was published last year, director Francis Lawrence ‘s movie carries a production budget of roughly $150 million as it revitalizes the franchise in telling a story set 24 years before the events of the original 2008 book.

This opening represents a major comeback for the series after registering its lowest-performing entry with 2023 prequel The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes , given that Sunrise on the Reaping is looking to open with more than double its launch. Starring Tom Blyth, Rachel Zegler and Hunter Schafer, Songbirds & Snakes — telling the backstory for the villainous President Snow, played by Ralph Fiennes in the new movie — disappointed in opening to $44 million domestically for the weekend before ending its run with $166.4 million domestically and a global sum of $361.8 million. It earned a B+ CinemaScore, the lowest for the franchise.

Sunrise on the Reaping holds a 67 critical score on Rotten Tomatoes as it lags behind the franchise’s first four movies but bests the 64 percent approval for Songbirds & Snakes . The new film has a 95 audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. In his review for The Hollywood Reporter , chief film critic David Rooney wrote that it “delivers on emotion and brutal spectacle.”

entertainment.title: 10 Fantasy Shows Every Harry Potter Fan Needs To Watch
entertainment.summary: Harry Potter isn't the only franchise revolving around arcane schools and young protagonists from humble origins learning of their true potential.
entertainment.body:
Aidan Monaghan/HBO Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover "Harry Potter" has cast an everlasting spell on the fantasy genre. Now, with HBO's TV series anticipated to entertain Wizarding World aficionados for at least a decade, its popularity will likely continue to soar. However, fantasy fans might need a fix while they wait for new seasons to arrive, as 10 years is a long time. The good news, though, is that there are plenty of shows out there that will scratch one's proverbial "Harry Potter" itch.

On this list, you will find great fantasy shows hang out in the same wheelhouse as J.K. Rowling's saga — whether that's through storylines, themes, characters, or all of the above. Some are likeminded YA stories about young heroes teaming up to save the world from the forces of darkness. Others are more adult-oriented. Regardless of their approach, they all feature all of the magic and wonder that makes "Harry Potter" so appealing to millions of people.

Of course, no one wants to watch a show that's completely derivative of something else. These series all echo "Harry Potter" in some ways, but they also highlight the diverse nature of the fantasy genre as a whole. With that said, here are 10 great shows that every Wizarding World aficionado should add to their watchlist.

Sky One Tell us if you've heard this story before: A person with magical abilities is burdened by the death of their parents. They live in a fantastical world that's governed by a strict order who want magical beings to remain separate from humans. Meanwhile, the central characters attend a famous academic institution that's known for producing legends. Yep, we're talking about "A Discovery of Witches."

"A Discovery of Witches" centers around Diana Bishop (Teresa Palmer), an Oxford historian, and Matthew Clairmont (Matthew Goode), a religious type, after the former discovers an arcane manuscript. Now that the magical text has been unearthed, every creature in the world is after it, forcing our protagonists to band together. Oh, and did we mention that Diana is a witch and Matthew is a vampire who develop the hots for each other? Let's just say that's frowned upon in their circles.

It would be easy to dismiss "A Discovery of Witches" as "Harry Potter" meets "Twilight," but that's a reductive take. Yes, the show is reminiscent of J.K. Rowling's stories and it leans into interspecies romance, but there's so much more to it. This world is loaded with fascinating political intrigue and world-building, with each episode full of drama and adventure. Besides that, the love story is a great one, as Goode and Palmer's chemistry pops off the screen.

entertainment.body:
Kate Middleton is shedding light on one of her darkest chapters.

The Princess of Wales shared a vulnerable glimpse into her cancer journey in the trailer for her upcoming documentary Heal , detailing how her 2024 diagnosis fundamentally altered her life forever.

“Cancer does change you,” Kate—who publicly shared her diagnosis in March 2024—said in the trailer released Nov. 21. “It changes your body. It changes you physically. But there's a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The documentary, available on NBC Nov. 30, follows Kate as she undertakes the National Three Peaks Challenge, climbing the highest mountains in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours in support of The Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which funds cancer treatment and research.

In one clip, Kate informed her brother James Middleton that she “didn’t ring the bell” when she learned she was cancer free in September 2024, to which he replied, “Maybe this is your ringing of the bell.” (Kate announced that she was in remission in January 2025.)

Throughout the physically demanding trek, which Kate completed this past June, the 44-year-old not only reflected on her own experience with the disease, but she also connected with others who are navigating their own health battles.

“You know, healing is a journey,” she said. “How to reconnect with the things you once knew, and how to find a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty.”

“It's clear we're not meant to carry life's challenges alone,” she added. “Things can renew and grow. Often, it is through pain that we realize there's a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”

entertainment.title: The Making of My Chemical Romance’s ‘The Black Parade’
entertainment.summary: After the return of My Chemical Romance's classic third album to the top of the charts, producer Rob Cavallo looks back at the wild tale of its creation, from a haunted mansion to Liza Minelli
entertainment.body:
My Chemical Romance didn’t waste a minute of their way-too-abbreviated recording career, making one of rock’s last great concept albums on their third try in the studio, 2006’s The Black Parade. It was Tommy in a white belt and eyeliner, vastly expanding the band’s sonic palette beyond the punk-thrash of their first two albums. It felt like the beginning of what should have been a long, ambitious new phase of My Chem’s career, but instead, they released the underrated Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys in 2010 and broke up three years later.

Their welcome return to the road has yet to be accompanied by new music, but the band — frontman Gerard Way , lead guitarist and backing vocalist Ray Toro, rhythm guitarist Frank Iero, and bassist Mikey Way (drummer Bob Bryar left in 2010 and died in 2024) — is promising that will change soon.

Welcome to the Black Parade recently celebrated its 20th anniversary, and a new vinyl edition made a surprise Number One debut. That album’s producer, Rob Cavallo (who also worked on much of Green Day ‘s discography, among many other projects) joined Rolling Stone by Zoom for an in-depth look at the making of a 21st-century rock masterpiece.

What did My Chem first play for you that got you excited to be involved in this album? They were interviewing other guys as well, but I’ll never forget, ’cause it was so freezing cold in New York, and we went to SIR , and they played me a few things. But the one that blew my mind was “Mama.” When I heard that, I remember just jumping off the couch just going, “Oh, my God, you guys. That is so great and original,” and you could tell it was part of a deeper picture of something, even though I was new to the band. It felt important to me right away that this band was existing on a higher conceptual level.

That song sounds like the Doors version of “Alabama Song.” It’s very un-punk at first, and then it kicks into the— The heavy part, right. Yeah, I kinda likened it in a weird way rhythmically to the Doors. I was also thinking of [the Rolling Stones’] “Mother’s Little Helper.” Almost like you could see the Cossacks-style Russian dancing to it. It’s like this sort of head-bopping thing that just felt very edgy, and very anti-establishment rock in a weird way. It was definitely like the we-don’t-give-a-fuck kind of rock. entertainment.title: Why Spock's Father Beat Leonard Nimoy's Vulcan Hero To Star Trek: The Next Generation
entertainment.summary: Mark Lenard played Spock's father, Sarek, in just one episode of "Star Trek: The Original Series." But he still made it to "ST:TNG" before his TV son.
entertainment.body:
Paramount Domestic Television Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover As the title suggested, "Star Trek: The Next Generation" was about the next generation of Starfleet officers, the ones who came after Kirk and Company on "The Original Series." However, a few "TOS" characters did appear on "TNG," and while Spock did eventually show up, a Vulcan from an even older generation beat him to it. Spock's father, Sarek, appeared on "TNG" two seasons before Spock did, because the show couldn't afford Spock's actor, Leonard Nimoy .

Actor Mark Lenard played Spock's father in an episode of "TOS," reprising the role in "The Animated Series" and a few of the original "Star Trek" films. When "TNG" premiered in syndication in 1987, there wasn't initially a great clamoring for an episode that would bring Sarek back. However, as "TNG" writer and script coordinator Eric A. Stillwell explained in his book "The Making of Yesterday's Enterprise," series creator Gene Roddenberry "had distributed a memo to the writing staff at one point saying that due to financial considerations it would probably be impossible to ever entertain the idea of Leonard Nimoy guest starring." Stillwell said Roddenberry suggested Lenard's Sarek as "a reasonable alternative."

Stillwell and co-writer Trent Christopher Ganino originally intended for Sarek to feature in what became one of the 60 best "Star Trek" episodes , "Yesterday's Enterprise." Instead, that story became a means to bring Denise Crosby back to the show, as her character, Tasha Yar, had been killed off in Season 1 . Sarek instead appears later in Season 3, in the aptly titled episode "Sarek."

Paramount Domestic Television Spock eventually joined his father by appearing on "The Next Generation," but not until Season 5 and only because it happened to be a bit of mutually beneficial cross-promotion. The last of the original-series films, "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country," was set to hit theaters in December 1991. Nimoy was reprising his role as Spock on the big screen and had co-written and executive-produced the picture as well. On the small screen, "TNG" continued to be a success, and by this point had fully assuaged any fears that it would forever be overshadowed by "TOS." Frank Mancuso, chairman of Paramount, suggested having the movie and show promote one another.

"He got very little, a little more than scale," Berman said in "Star Trek: The Next Generation Companion," referring to the industry term for union salary minimum. "But with Leonard as executive producer of 'Star Trek VI,' what you had in essence was a cross-promotion. It made everybody happy."

entertainment.title: The '80s Reboot Of Sally Field's Beloved '60s Sitcom Lasted Longer Than The Original
entertainment.summary: Sally Field started out in TV, playing a beach-loving teen on a '60s sitcom. But the series ran for one season and the '80s reboot actually outlasted it.
entertainment.body:
While Field may be the most famous face of "Gidget," she wasn't the last to play the character. The series was relaunched in the 1980s with "The New Gidget," in which Caryn Richman played the title role. The reboot follows an adult, married Gidget as she looks after her mischievous niece, Danielle, or Dani for short (Sydney Penny). The show actually lasted longer than Field's series, airing, via syndication, for two seasons and 44 episodes.

Though Field's "Gidget" only lasted for one season, it eventually found its intended audience, which may explain why it's still so recognizable today. The series had strong viewership during summer reruns, when teens had more time for watching TV, and even made it into the top 10. Reruns continued to air for many years — a rarity for a single-season show — and ABC received angry letters from fans upon learning of its cancellation.

The poor reputation of "The Flying Nun" TV series made it difficult for Field to find the kind of roles she wanted. " I worked so hard to get out of television ," she told Parade in 2026. "People wouldn't let me in a room to audition." Eventually, Field's perseverance paid off, and she won her first Oscar in 1980 for playing a union organizer in the film "Norma Rae." She would later return to television, appearing in a memorable guest spot on "ER" and starring in the ABC drama "Brothers & Sisters."
